newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's troublesome unemployment rate falls.
newsitem.headline: Canada's troublesome unemployment rate falls.

text.p: Canada's unemployment rate, which had spiked into double digits in June, returned in August to the more usual level of 9.4 percent, Statistics Canada said on Friday.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien had characterised the rise in June to 10.0 percent as a mere "blip," but when it fell only to 9.8 percent in July, some eyebrows began to be raised.
"I finally exhaled after two months of wondering where the jobs were," Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce Senior Economist John Clinkard commented.
Chretien has relied for job creation mainly on lower interest rates stemming from steadily falling budget deficits.

"We're thrilled. The government is trying hard to put the fundamentals of the economy on track, and the unemployment rate just proves that what we're doing is right," Chretien spokeswoman Leslie Swartman told Reuters.
The 82,000 jobs created in August, to a total of 13.72 million, was the highest in more than three years and more than offset job losses in June. For the year to date, 153,000 jobs have been created.
The unemployment rate has fallen from a peak of 11.9 percent in late 1992 but Chretien has nonetheless been unable to push it below 9 percent.
Since October 1994 it has been stuck between 9 percent and 10 percent, nearly double the 5.1 percent reported on Friday in the United States, where job creation also was strong.

In the near term the better numbers here and in the United States made it more unlikely that the Bank of Canada, which had been aggressively lowering interest rates independent of U.S. rates, would push Canadian rates down further.
"Those prospects at this juncture have all but vanished," said senior economist David Rosenberg at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
"If you are lowering rates in advance of a potential U.S. increase, you put yourself at some risk," said Clinkard of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
The Canadian dollar opened a bit firmer at C$1.3712 to the U.S. dollar from Thursday's close of C$1.3730.

Rosenberg noted the 51,000 new jobs in Ontario, the manufacturing heartland of Canada, suggesting that this could help budget revenues to exceed expectations and possibly even help the bond market rather than harm it.
"My sense is that those revenue projections are being exceeded," echoed Clinkard.

The unemployment rate in Quebec, which is run by a separatist government, fell to 11.8 percent in August from 12.4 percent in July but job gains only partially offset estimated losses from June and July.
The Quebec government had reacted angrily to the numbers and suggested that Statistics Canada, a federal agency, had erred in arriving at the figures of the past two months.
